Empirical Research Plan  
“Does more‐intensive treatment of acute myocardial infarction (AMI) in the elderly reduce mortality?”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Two–stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental-variables (IV) design that instruments individual treatment intensity with exogenous variation in local “practice style.”

Why IV?  
• Treatment intensity is chosen by physicians conditional on unobserved patient severity → OLS is likely biased upward (sicker patients get more care).  
• Across hospitals/regions, large, persistent differences in how aggressively AMI is treated that are not obviously driven by any single patient’s characteristics.  
• These supply-side practice patterns can be exploited as quasi-random variation once we condition on rich Medicare covariates, geography, and year fixed effects.  
Alternative designs (DiD, RDD) would require a sharp policy change or a cutoff that is not present here; IV cleanly targets the cross-sectional practice-style variation that is already known to exist in AMI care.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control Definitions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable (Tᵢ): Indicator =1 if patient i received an “intensive” AMI intervention during the index hospitalization or within 30 days (e.g., immediate catheterization, PCI, CABG, thrombolytics administered in-hospital). A continuous version (number of intensive procedures or Medicare spending in first 30 days, winsorized at 99th pct) will be used as robustness.

Instrument (Zᵢ): Hospital-year “leave-one-out” mean intensive-treatment rate for AMI patients:
 Zᵢ = (1/N_{ht,-i}) ∑_{j≠i} T_{j},  where hospital h treated patient i in year t.  
This is a classic “predicted treatment” or practice-style instrument.

Control group / counterfactual: Patients whose instrument predicts low intensity (bottom quartile of Z) but who are otherwise observationally similar.

Treatment timing: Index AMI admission date (t=0). Outcomes: 30-day and 1-year mortality.

No running variable or cutoff (not an RDD).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1 (Relevance). Hospital-year practice style strongly predicts individual treatment intensity (first-stage F > 10). Plausible given large observed variation.

A2 (Exclusion / Independence). Conditional on rich controls (age, sex, race, comorbidities, AMI severity dummies, ZIP×year FE, and hospital capacity measures), the hospital’s practice style affects mortality only through the patient’s own treatment intensity.  
• Plausible because it is defined entirely by other AMI patients, but could fail if high-intensity hospitals are also generally higher quality. Addressed below.

A3 (Monotonicity). Patients admitted to a more‐intense hospital are at least as likely (never less likely) to receive intensive care. Reasonable: a high-intensity hospital will not discourage intensive care for any patient relative to a low-intensity hospital.

A4 (SUTVA / no spillovers). One patient’s instrument does not affect another’s outcome beyond its effect on that patient’s treatment. Reasonable within AMI context.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigations
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Non-random sorting of patients to hospitals (e.g., ambulances divert the sickest to tertiary centers).  
• Mitigation: Restrict sample to emergency admissions from patient’s home ZIP where the closest hospital treats ≥ 5 AMIs per year; include ZIP×year fixed effects so comparisons are within very small geographies.  
• Use “differential distance” robustness: instrument with (distance to nearest high-intensity hospital minus distance to nearest low-intensity hospital).

Threat 2: Exclusion restriction violated if high-intensity hospitals have better nursing ratios, ICUs, or post-AMI care that directly lowers mortality.  
• Mitigation: Control flexibly for hospital technology, nurse-to-bed ratio, teaching status, and 30-day risk-standardized mortality for unrelated diagnoses (e.g., hip fracture).  
• Conduct placebo test: re-estimate IV effect on 30-day mortality for diagnoses whose treatment intensity is uncorrelated with the AMI instrument (e.g., pneumonia). No effect supports exclusion.

Threat 3: Measurement error in defining “intensive” care. Misclassification will weaken first stage.  
• Mitigation: (i) use multiple definitions (procedure indicator, spending, DRG weight), (ii) report first-stage F for each, (iii) show consistent reduced-form effect of instrument on mortality.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
#-------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
#-------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast IV / FE
library(modelsummary)

#-------------------------------------------
# 1. Load Data
#-------------------------------------------
df <- fread("medicare_ami.csv")   # assume one row per AMI admission

#-------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable Construction
#-------------------------------------------
# Intensive treatment indicator: any PCI, CABG, thrombolytic, or cath
df[, intensive := (pci==1 | cabg==1 | thrombolytic==1 | cath==1)]

# 30-day and 1-year mortality
df[, death30  := (death_date <= admit_date + 30)]
df[, death365 := (death_date <= admit_date + 365)]

# Hospital-year practice-style instrument (leave-one-out)
df[, Z := (sum(intensive) - intensive) / ( .N - 1 ), by = .(hospital_id, year)]

# Optional differential-distance instrument
# df[, Z_dist := ddist_highintensity - ddist_lowintensity]

#-------------------------------------------
# 3. Controls
#-------------------------------------------
ctrls <- c("age", "I(age^2)", "female", "black", "hispanic",
           "charlson_index", "stemi", "nsti", 
           "zip_fe", "year_fe")   # zip and year fixed effects created below

# Factor dummies
df[, zip_fe  := factor(zip)]
df[, year_fe := factor(year)]

#-------------------------------------------
# 4. 2SLS Estimation
#-------------------------------------------
# Main specification: death30 on intensive, IV = Z, FE: zip×year
iv_formula <- as.formula(
  paste("death30 ~ intensive | Z +", paste(ctrls[-c(10,11)], collapse = " + "),
        "+ zip_fe + year_fe") )

mod_iv <- feols(iv_formula, data = df, cluster = "hospital_id")
etable(mod_iv, se = "cluster")

#-------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: OLS, alternative instrument, placebo
#-------------------------------------------
# OLS (naïve)
mod_ols <- feols(death30 ~ intensive + age + I(age^2) + female + black + hispanic +
                 charlson_index + stemi + nsti + zip_fe + year_fe,
                 data = df, cluster = "hospital_id")

# Alternative instrument: differential distance
# mod_iv2 <- feols(death30 ~ intensive | Z_dist + ... , data=df, cluster="hospital_id")

# Placebo outcome: 30-day mortality from pneumonia admissions in same hospitals
# pneu <- fread("medicare_pneumonia.csv")
# ... run same IV using AMI practice-style Z on pneumonia mortality

modelsummary(list(OLS = mod_ols, IV = mod_iv), stars = TRUE)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic/medical theory suggests that timely invasive therapy improves perfusion, limits heart-muscle death, and thereby improves survival. Therefore:

Hypothesized sign: β_IV < 0 (intensive care lowers mortality).  
Magnitude: Baseline 30-day mortality ≈ 20 %. A 100 pp increase in intensive treatment (conceptually) might reduce mortality by ~8 pp; the local average treatment effect (moving a marginal patient from conservative to intensive care) is likely around −2 to −3 percentage points (10–15 % relative decline).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV Method)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1 Strong first stage (F > 10): 1  
C2 Instrument exogenous (Independence): 0.5 (good controls but some concern)  
C3 Exclusion restriction: 0.5 (hospital quality could matter)  
C4 SUTVA / no spillovers: 1  
C5 Monotonicity (no defiers): 1  

Total = 4 / 5 – credible but not bulletproof; careful robustness and falsification tests are essential.
